prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands at the magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene, founding moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the clearest recent case of a quantitative theoretical prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, 2011) followed by a decisive and surprising experiment (correlated insulators and superconductivity, 2018). It is a new state-of-matter platform in a single tunable carbon material, and it has spawned a whole family of moire systems. The physics is tied to transport and spectroscopy, and the continuum model can be checked against DFT and tight-binding calculations, which is the kind of quantitative, verifiable link between theory and measurement that I look for. Seven of eight members ranked it, four in the top three, and two ranked it first, so it has broad committee support as well as my own.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity of interpretation. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unsettled, the correlated phases are sensitive to twist-angle disorder and strain, and reproducibility across samples is uneven. The discovery itself is secure, but a prize framed around superconductivity could age badly. The credit problem is also real: the experimental first author (Yuan Cao) and parallel groups such as Dean, Young, Yazdani and Efetov are outside the credited names, and the three-person limit forces a choice. If the committee judges that the timing is early, B015 is the safer, more mature choice, and I would not stand in the way of it.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B006 first because a minimal continuum model predicts the magic-angle flattening, so the mechanism is understood and not only observed, and he regards the timing as timely rather than premature.
responses.response: I agree on the value of a simple mechanism, but I would qualify the word understood. The single-particle flat band is well understood and quantitatively tested; the many-body states that emerge from it are not, and the superconducting pairing is still contested. I would therefore keep the citation anchored on the flat-band prediction and the observation of the correlated states, and avoid any wording that implies a settled mechanism for the superconductivity.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B015 first as a clean, robust, easily explained precision result, and rates B006 only fourth because the many-body physics is not settled and sample variation is large. She also says B055 is distinct from the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I take her maturity point seriously; it is the strongest argument against my own first choice, and on robustness B015 is clearly ahead. I still hold that a new tunable state-of-matter platform with an explicit theory-to-experiment chain is closer to what the physics prize has recognised in condensed matter. On B055 I agree with her that time-reversal-invariant topological insulators were not covered in 2016, which is why it is my second choice. I do not accept that the unresolved pairing mechanism should disqualify B006, since the existence of the phases is not in doubt.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B015 first because progress in physics is limited by how precisely we can measure, with agreement between independent labs at the 1e-18 level and a pending redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree that B015 is mature and very well confirmed, and that its attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist. Where I differ is on the overlap worry that he also raises himself: the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-clock prize cover much of the enabling physics, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. I would accept B015 if the committee prefers it, but I would like us to test whether it adds enough beyond those two prizes before it is treated as the default.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B013 first as a genuine, overwhelmingly confirmed invention that has changed an entire instrument class, and says recognition is overdue.
responses.response: I ranked B013 sixth, so I share her respect for it, and as someone whose theory depends on atomic-resolution structure data I value what aberration correction has done for materials. My reservation is the physics-versus-instrumentation question, and that the STEM corrector line (Krivanek and Dellby) is omitted, which makes the three-name credit less fair than it appears. I would keep it as a strong candidate for a later cycle rather than this one.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a prize before the superconducting pairing mechanism is understood, or wait.
How to handle the credited-name limit when the experimental first author (Cao) and parallel experimental groups are outside the supplied names.
Whether the 2016 topological prize reduces appetite for B055 enough that B006 or B015 is the better use of this year.
Whether B015 adds enough beyond the 2005 and 2012 prizes to be treated as the consensus choice.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. B006 and B055 are in my broad field of condensed-matter theory, but I have no stated personal or institutional link to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp, and I am not aware of a co-authorship or supervisory tie.
